segments.text: SpaceX will attempt to catch both the super heavy booster and starship upper stage on flight 15. A dual catch would be the first full recovery of an orbital launch vehicle. This is SpaceX Daily, Episode 137. Quarterly results, Tesla merger committees, and a vandenberg scrub follow. Then the counterpoint, the ai front, and the engineering deep dive. Flight 15 is expected next month, and the launch tower arms are assigned to both stages, according to keeptrack.space.
An 82nd animation from the earnings webcast showed the Starship upper stage finishing its belly flop,
steering with forward and aft flaps at the nose and tail, then swinging vertical.
The arms grab it after the upper stage drops past the tower top.
Elon Musk said the first try is more likely than not to work.
SpaceX is keeping Starship flights coming through the end of the year if that try fails.
Gwynne Shotwell described SpaceX's third quarter results in which connectivity kept climbing
and Starship started to haul more.
The company reported $14.6 billion of revenue, a 161% rise from the same quarter last year.
The connectivity segment posted 69% revenue growth and 99% growth in income from operations,
helped by enterprise, government, and consumer starlink adoption.
Shotwell said Starship Flight 14 delivered 26 Starlink version 3 satellites.
Those satellites provide roughly 10 times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 Starlink launch.
The service was active across 174 markets, with hundreds of thousands of additional enterprise and aviation customers.
SpaceX and Tesla each set up a special committee of independent directors to study a possible merger.
Elon Musk called the combination a good idea on the earnings call.

star-mind constellation and connectivity. Musk said he supports combining the two
largest companies. He stated there is a lot of merit to combining them as they
are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity. The review follows SpaceX
acquiring XAI in February and going public in June. Van den Berg's Space Force
base scrubbed a planned Falcon 9 Starlink launch after a technical issue. Spaceflight now reports.
The mission was to carry 27 Starlink satellites on October 20th using a booster on its 36th flight.
It is now targeted for a window opening at 259 pm Pacific time on October 21st.
The booster is slated to land on the drone ship a shortfall of gravitas. That would be landing
number 229 for that ship, and Falcon booster landing number 673.
The rocket will fly on a south-easterly trajectory, and roughly eight and a half minutes after
liftoff, the booster will target the drone ship if the attempt proceeds.

Fatalites have been launched, 11,154 are in orbit, and 11,140 are operational in low

SpaceX added 1.6 million subscribers in the third quarter, 10 upcoming Starlink conjunctions,
meaning predicted close approaches, appear in the current Socrates collision probability

Japan, and China.

Earnings materials show nameplate compute capacity, the labeled peak draw of the installed machines
at 1.7 gigawatts as of September 30th, while Starship remains the primary capital consumer.
Sustaining that investment with a plan 35-40 billion-dollar fourth-quarter capital expenditure
run rate will test whether AI and connectivity revenue can scale fast enough to support continued

On the AI front, SpaceX added $6.7 billion-year-over-year from superintelligence solutions and infrastructure,

Cloud Services Agreements, the acquisition of Cursor, and growth in superintelligence models
and software applications, including GROC, drove that increment.
Public filings now place most expected future revenue in AI-related business.
The company described the AI segment as overtaking Starlink on some internal contribution measures
during the quarter.
AI business revenue surged 830% in the quarter.
For that flight 15 upper-stage catch, the engineering reality is converting hypersonic
high-drag flight into a vertical capture only seconds before contact.
The flaps steer the belly flop, then the Raptor engines relight to flip the stage upright
and break.
Those flaps have to raise pitch and yaw while the starship upper-stage is still moving
at hundreds of meters per second.
The flip and the landing burn have to be timed so the stage arrives inside the arm geometry
envelope.
horizontal velocity and leftover rates have to die away before the arms close
and the landing burn does the last of that work. The upper stage has no super
heavy-style grid fins and body flap bite collapses below a few kilopascals of
dynamic pressure. That pressure is one-half times air density times velocity
squared. Near the ground density is about 1.2 kilograms per cubic meter. At 100
meters per second you get on the order of 6 kilopascals. At 50 meters per second you
get about 1.5 kilopascals. Authority falls with the square of speed, so the flaps go
mushy faster than the vehicle slows. Right into the flip. That square law is why the last
second is the whole game. Hypersonic means faster than Mach 5 on the order of a kilometer
and a half per second or more, before drag bleeds it down. At vertical residual horizontal
speed and pitch and yaw rates have to be small enough for the arms and the skirt to take the load.
SpaceX has not published the limits. Twice the leftover speed is not twice the problem. Energy and
therefore load go with velocity squared, so it is four times the hit. A leftover rotation turns a
straight compressive load into a peel on the arm pins. Structural steel yields on the order of
a few hundred megapascals, so a side slip at remaining descent speed is a spike, not a tap.
The flaps steer the descent, but the last seconds belong to the engines.
The stage relights its raptors to flip upright and break, and the arms take what is left.
The controller trims that burn into the last half-second before capture.
At 40 meters per second of descent, that half-second is on the order of 20 meters of travel.
The arms are a fixed geometry and cannot chase a miss, so the vehicle has to fly into
a box measured in meters.
measures. Ground tests cannot stack reentry heat soak, falling dynamic pressure and flight
mass properties in one article, so the first attempt is the first combined margin data.
Expendable upper stages have always been the accepted waste in this business. The Shuttle
Orbiter bought reuse with wings and a runway and paid for it in dry mass. Repeatable
starship upper stage recovery would drop a second heat shielded system, and the propellant
and otherwise spent discarding the stage.
The idiot index of a thrown away ship, the finished article over stainless sheet and
methalox, stays high until you catch it.
Dual use flaps must survive peak heating and still provide pitch in low dynamic pressure,
so the design wants more area and faster actuators than reentry steering alone would ever need.
